learn.hook: Your heartbeat, a jhoola at a mela, the hands of a clock and atoms in a crystal: all repeat their motion again and again.
points: Periodic and oscillatory motions are everywhere: swings, pendulums, heartbeats, vibrating strings and atoms in solids.
Oscillations underlie sound, waves of all kinds and alternating currents in electrical circuits.
Periodic motion repeats itself at regular intervals of time (the Earth's rotation, a clock's hands).

Oscillatory (vibratory) motion is to-and-fro motion about a mean (equilibrium) position. Every oscillatory motion is periodic, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory (uniform circular motion is periodic, not to-and-fro).
Oscillations happen because a restoring force acts towards the equilibrium position whenever the body is displaced.

example.q: Classify (a) the Moon going round the Earth and (b) a swinging jhoola.
steps: (a) The Moon repeats its path every 27.3 days, but does not move to and fro about a mean position: periodic, not oscillatory.
(b) The jhoola moves to and fro about its lowest point at regular intervals: oscillatory (and hence periodic).

learn.reallife: The quartz crystal in a digital watch oscillates 32768 times a second, keeping time for millions of Indians' wrists.

learn.hook: Indian classical tabla rhythms, alternating current at 50 Hz and a pendulum clock all have one thing in common: a definite period.
points: Period T: the smallest time after which the motion repeats. Frequency ν = 1/T (unit hertz, Hz = s⁻¹).
The displacement variable need not be a position. It can be an angle (pendulum), pressure (sound), voltage or current (AC), or electric and magnetic fields (light).
Any periodic function can be built as a sum of sines and cosines of different periods (Fourier's idea).

Checking periodicity: sin ωt, cos ωt and sin ωt + cos ωt are periodic with T = 2π/ω; sin²ωt is periodic with T = π/ω; sin ωt + cos 2ωt is periodic with T = 2π/ω (but not SHM); e^(−ωt) and log(ωt) are not periodic.

example.q: Find the period of x(t) = sin ωt + sin 2ωt.
steps: sin ωt has period 2π/ω; sin 2ωt has period π/ω.
The sum repeats only when both repeat.

topics.title: Simple harmonic motion: displacement, amplitude and phase

learn.hook: A child on a spring rider at a park bounces up and down in a beautifully regular way. That motion is (nearly) simple harmonic.
points: SHM: displacement varies sinusoidally with time: x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ).
A = amplitude (maximum displacement, positive). (ωt + φ) = phase; φ = phase constant (epoch), the phase at t = 0. ω = angular frequency = 2π/T = 2πν.
On x–t graphs: a larger A gives taller curves; a different φ shifts the curve along the time axis; a larger ω squeezes it (shorter period).
To write the SHM equation, read A, T (hence ω) and the value of x at t = 0 (hence φ).

example.q: A particle in SHM has amplitude 5 cm and period 2 s, and starts at x = +5 cm at t = 0. Write x(t).
steps: A = 5 cm, ω = 2π/T = π rad s⁻¹.
At t = 0, x = A, so cos φ = 1 → φ = 0.

learn.reallife: Seismographs at IMD stations record ground vibrations as sinusoids; their amplitude and period reveal an earthquake's strength and distance.

topics.title: SHM as the projection of uniform circular motion

learn.hook: Shine a torch on a bead going round a turntable and watch its shadow on the wall: the shadow moves back and forth in perfect SHM.
points: If a particle moves uniformly on a circle, its projection (foot of the perpendicular) on any diameter executes SHM.
Reference circle: radius of the circle = amplitude A; angular speed of the particle = angular frequency ω of the SHM; initial angle = phase constant φ.
If the particle starts at angle φ from the x-axis and moves anticlockwise, its x-projection is x = A cos(ωt + φ) and its y-projection is y = A sin(ωt + φ).
Uniform circular motion = two perpendicular SHMs of equal amplitude with a phase difference of π/2.

example.q: A particle moves anticlockwise on a circle of radius 3 cm at 2 rev s⁻¹, starting at 60° from the +x axis. Write the SHM of its x-projection.
steps: A = 3 cm; ω = 2π × 2 = 4π rad s⁻¹; φ = π/3.

learn.reallife: Try it at home: put a cup near the edge of a slowly turning lazy-susan tray and shine a torch across the tray, level with it. The cup's shadow on the wall slides to and fro in SHM.

learn.hook: A pendulum bob is fastest as it swings through the bottom and momentarily stops at the ends, where its acceleration is greatest.
points: Velocity: v = dx/dt = −ωA sin(ωt + φ). Maximum speed ωA at the mean position; zero at the extremes.
Speed in terms of displacement: v = ω√(A² − x²).
Acceleration: a = −ω²A cos(ωt + φ) = −ω²x. It always points towards the mean position; maximum magnitude ω²A at the extremes, zero at the mean position.
Phase relations: velocity leads displacement by π/2; acceleration leads displacement by π (opposite to x).
Typical problems: find v_max = ωA and a_max = ω²A.

topics.title: The force law: springs and SHM

learn.hook: Stiffer shock absorbers on a mountain bike bounce faster. The period of a spring–mass system depends on the ratio m/k.
points: Force law for SHM: F = ma = −mω²x = −kx, with k = mω². The restoring force is linear in displacement and opposite to it.
So ω = √(k/m) and T = 2π√(m/k).
A block of mass m on a spring of constant k on a frictionless surface is a linear harmonic oscillator.
Two identical springs (each k) attached to a block on opposite sides: displacing the block by x stretches one and compresses the other, so F = −2kx, k_eff = 2k and T = 2π√(m/2k).
Typical problem: given k and m, find T, then a_max = (k/m)A and v_max = A√(k/m).

example.q: A 1 kg block on a spring of k = 100 N m⁻¹ oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m. Find T, v_max and a_max (π = 3.14).
example.answer: T ≈ 0.63 s; 1 m s⁻¹; 10 m s⁻²

learn.reallife: The suspension springs of an auto-rickshaw are chosen so that the bounce period is comfortable for passengers on bumpy roads.

learn.hook: A swing at the top of its arc is all potential energy; at the bottom it's all kinetic. The total never changes (if there's no friction).
points: Kinetic energy K = ½mv² = ½kA² sin²(ωt + φ). Potential energy U = ½kx² = ½kA² cos²(ωt + φ).
Total energy E = K + U = ½kA², constant. Energy keeps changing between kinetic and potential forms.
K and U each oscillate in time with period T/2 (twice per cycle), between 0 and ½kA².
Against displacement: U(x) = ½kx² is a parabola, K(x) = ½k(A² − x²) an inverted parabola; E is a horizontal line. K = U at x = ±A/√2.

example.q: A block (k = 200 N m⁻¹) oscillates with A = 0.1 m. Find E, and K and U at x = 0.05 m.

learn.hook: Galileo timed a swinging chandelier with his pulse and noticed something surprising: big or small swings, the time was the same.
points: A simple pendulum is a point mass (bob) hung from a light, inextensible string fixed at one end.
When displaced by θ, gravity gives a restoring torque τ = −mgL sin θ about the support.
For small angles, sin θ ≈ θ (in radians), so τ = −mgLθ: angular acceleration ∝ −θ, which is SHM.
Period T = 2π√(L/g). It is independent of the mass of the bob and (for small oscillations) of the amplitude.

example.q: Find the period of a pendulum of length 0.4 m (g = 9.8 m s⁻², π = 3.14).

learn.reallife: Pendulum clocks once kept time in Indian railway stations; adjusting the bob's height (L) corrected the clock.

topics.title: Seconds pendulum, measuring g and other SHMs

learn.hook: The 'seconds pendulum' takes exactly one second for each swing from one side to the other. Its length on Earth works out to very nearly 1 metre.
points: A seconds pendulum has a period of 2 s (each swing, one side to the other, takes 1 s). Its length L = gT²/(4π²) ≈ 0.99 m ≈ 1 m.
Measuring g: time many oscillations to find T, then g = 4π²L/T². Plotting T² against L gives a straight line of slope 4π²/g.
In a lift accelerating upward at a, the effective g is (g + a), so T decreases; accelerating downward, (g − a), T increases; in free fall, the pendulum does not oscillate.
On the Moon (g_Moon ≈ g/6), T is √6 times longer.

Other SHMs: a ball rolling in a smooth bowl near the bottom, liquid oscillating in a U-tube, a mass on springs. The Earth's rotation is periodic but not SHM; a polyatomic molecule's general vibration is a superposition of SHMs.

example.q: Find the length of a seconds pendulum where g = 9.8 m s⁻² (π² ≈ 9.87).

learn.reallife: Students in CBSE physics labs across India find g by timing 20 oscillations of a pendulum of known length; the class average is usually close to 9.8 m s⁻². Lab safety: clamp the stand firmly so it can't tip, and keep the swing small and clear of faces.
